title: Immunoinformatics and reverse vaccinology design of self-amplifying RNA vaccine against marburg virus with structural dynamics and immune simulation analysis
abstract: Marburg virus disease (MVD), a deadly zoonotic illness in humans, is caused by the Marburg virus (MARV), a single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Orthomarburgvirus genus of the Filoviridae family. There are currently no approved vaccines or efficient antiviral therapies for MARV, despite high morbidity and fatality rates of the virus, particularly in Africa. Recognizing its epidemic potential and its inclusion on the WHO list of blueprint priority pathogens, an immunoinformatics approach was used to design novel multi-epitope saRNA vaccine candidates (MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII) targeting the viral GP, NP, VP40, and VP35 via CD8 + , CD4 + , and B cell epitopes. These epitopes were derived from target protein sequences and incorporated into MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII after validation for antigenicity, non-allergenicity, non-toxicity, and conservation. Additionally, the selected epitopes were conjugated to suitable adjuvants via various linkers, thereby enabling the design of a potentially stable vaccine. Additionally, the designed MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII were incorporated into the standard saRNA model, in which ORF-2 encodes the target vaccine peptide. Moreover, biophysical analyses unveiled that the developed vaccines are basic (pI < 7), soluble (GRAVY < 0), and stable (aliphatic index < 80). Subsequently, docking of MB-saVaxI to TLR2 (-938.3) and TLR4 (-902.4), and MB-saVaxII to TLR3 (-1485.4) and TLR7 (-1543.6) demonstrated significant affinity, with detailed hydrogen-bond interactions validated by MM-GBSA and molecular dynamics simulations. Furthermore, MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII were effectively cloned in-silico into Escherichia coli, and immune simulations indicated that the vaccines triggered robust innate and adaptive immunity, with a sustained memory response and TH cell activation, as evidenced by IFN-γ and IL-2 production. Additionally, the mRNA structure of MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII remained stable throughout the expression pathway in the host. However, extensive in-vitro and in-vivo studies are needed to establish the safety and efficacy of this vaccine candidate conclusively.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the lack of effective vaccines or antiviral therapies for Marburg virus (MARV), a deadly zoonotic illness. The research sought to design novel multi-epitope self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) vaccine candidates targeting the viral GP, NP, VP40, and VP35 via CD8 + , CD4 + , and B cell epitopes.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved the design and in-silico cloning of two saRNA vaccine candidates (MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII) into the standard saRNA model, incorporating validated epitopes and suitable adjuvants. The study did not involve human or animal participants.
analysis.methods: The study utilized immunoinformatics approaches to identify and validate epitopes, conjugate them to adjuvants, and incorporate them into the saRNA model. Biophysical analyses were conducted to assess the stability and solubility of the vaccines. Immune simulations were performed to evaluate the potential immune response.
analysis.main_results: The study demonstrated significant affinity of the designed vaccines to TLR2, TLR3, TLR4, and TLR7, with detailed hydrogen-bond interactions validated by molecular dynamics simulations. The vaccines triggered robust innate and adaptive immune responses, evidenced by IFN-γ and IL-2 production, and remained stable throughout the expression pathway in the host.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the findings as novel and promising, indicating the potential for the designed vaccines to elicit strong immune responses. The study highlighted the use of immunoinformatics and reverse vaccinology in the design of saRNA vaccines against MARV.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings could inform the development of effective vaccines against MARV, contributing to the prevention and control of Marburg virus disease. The study's approach may also be applicable to other filoviruses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the need for extensive in-vitro and in-vivo studies to establish the safety and efficacy of the vaccine candidates conclusively. The evidence strength is moderate due to the in-silico nature of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to design novel multi-epitope saRNA vaccines against Marburg virus using immunoinformatics. The vaccines showed significant affinity to TLRs and triggered robust immune responses in immune simulations. Further in-vitro and in-vivo studies are needed to establish their safety and efficacy.

title_zh: 通过结构动力学和免疫模拟分析,针对 马尔堡病毒 自扩增 RNA 疫苗 进行免疫信息学和反向疫苗学设计
source_body_en: Marburg virus disease (MVD), a deadly zoonotic illness in humans, is caused by the Marburg virus (MARV), a single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the Orthomarburgvirus genus of the Filoviridae family. There are currently no approved vaccines or efficient antiviral therapies for MARV, despite high morbidity and fatality rates of the virus, particularly in Africa. Recognizing its epidemic potential and its inclusion on the WHO list of blueprint priority pathogens, an immunoinformatics approach was used to design novel multi-epitope saRNA vaccine candidates (MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII) targeting the viral GP, NP, VP40, and VP35 via CD8 + , CD4 + , and B cell epitopes. These epitopes were derived from target protein sequences and incorporated into MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII after validation for antigenicity, non-allergenicity, non-toxicity, and conservation. Additionally, the selected epitopes were conjugated to suitable adjuvants via various linkers, thereby enabling the design of a potentially stable vaccine. Additionally, the designed MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII were incorporated into the standard saRNA model, in which ORF-2 encodes the target vaccine peptide. Moreover, biophysical analyses unveiled that the developed vaccines are basic (pI < 7), soluble (GRAVY < 0), and stable (aliphatic index < 80). Subsequently, docking of MB-saVaxI to TLR2 (-938.3) and TLR4 (-902.4), and MB-saVaxII to TLR3 (-1485.4) and TLR7 (-1543.6) demonstrated significant affinity, with detailed hydrogen-bond interactions validated by MM-GBSA and molecular dynamics simulations. Furthermore, MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII were effectively cloned in-silico into Escherichia coli, and immune simulations indicated that the vaccines triggered robust innate and adaptive immunity, with a sustained memory response and TH cell activation, as evidenced by IFN-γ and IL-2 production. Additionally, the mRNA structure of MB-saVaxI and MB-saVaxII remained stable throughout the expression pathway in the host. However, extensive in-vitro and in-vivo studies are needed to establish the safety and efficacy of this vaccine candidate conclusively.

title: Filovirus Seroreactivity Beyond Virus-Specific Outbreak Regions in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, 2015-2023
abstract: The ongoing Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is the second-largest Ebola disease outbreak in recorded history, and only the second recorded BVD outbreak in the country. While the DRC has recorded 18 filovirus disease outbreaks, the historical frequency and geographic distribution of human filovirus exposures remain poorly understood. Using a multiplexed multi-filovirus immunoassay, we assessed antibody reactivity against antigens of filoviruses linked to human disease, Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), Ebola virus (EBOV), Marburg virus (MARV), and Sudan virus (SUDV), among eleven cohorts from seven provinces between 2015-2023 (n=5,852). Participants with median fluorescence intensity values exceeding established antigen-specific cutoffs were classified as seroreactive. Seroreactivity against glycoprotein (GP) targets of all four viruses were detected in every cohort, demonstrating evidence of filovirus or an antigenically related exposure well beyond known outbreak regions. Seroreactivity estimates varied by cohort site, with 60.8% of participants (n=175/288) in Mongala Province in April 2016 considered seroreactive against BDBV GP. In this cohort, 4.2%, 29.9%, and 34.7% of participants were seroreactive against EBOV, MARV and SUDV GP, respectively yet only 1.7% were seroreactive against all four GP antigens. In adjusted analyses, site was the primary predictor of seroreactivity, with odds for BDBV seroreactivity 9.1-fold (95%CI 7.0-11.9) and 9.5-fold (95%CI 6.9-13.2) higher in Mongala and Tshuapa provinces than in Kwilu. Similarly, the adjusted odds of MARV and SUDV GP seroreactivity were 4.5-fold and 7.1-fold higher in Mongala, and 3.7-fold and 6.1-fold higher in Tshuapa, than Kwilu. Among 280 individuals sampled longitudinally, BDBV GP detected seroconversion was comparable by site, with 12.8% in Kwilu and 10.4% in Mongala having detected seroreactivity three and five years after initial contact, respectively. Overall, these results indicate widespread, geographically heterogeneous filovirus seroreactivity across sampled cohorts. These findings may reflect zoonotic spillover events, leading to undetected human-to-human filovirus circulation, including paucisymptomatic or asymptomatic infections, or exposure to as-yet unidentified antigenically cross-reactive viruses. These data highlight gaps in understanding the historical and geographic distribution of filovirus exposure in the DRC and support further prospective serological, epidemiological, and molecular investigations, especially given the current outbreak.

title: Structure and antigenicity of the 2026 Bundibugyo virus glycoprotein
abstract: An outbreak of ebolavirus disease caused by a new zoonotic spillover of Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) is currently spreading at an unprecedented pace in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda. The outbreak has resulted in 7,733 cases with a case-fatality ratio of 48%, yet no BDBV-specific vaccines or therapeutics are available. The ebolavirus glycoprotein (GP) promotes viral entry and is the target of neutralizing antibodies and vaccine development. Here, we engineered a soluble, prefusion-stabilized GP trimer from a contemporary BDBV isolate and determined its cryo-electron microscopy structure bound to the broadly neutralizing antibody EBOV-515. It reveals the molecular basis for EBOV-515 cross-reactivity and suggests that the antibody inhibits viral entry by interfering with NPC1 engagement in addition to trapping GP in the prefusion conformation and hindering glycan cap cleavage. Mapping lineage-defining substitutions identified changes in GP1 and GP2, including R506S within an antigenic site targeted by multiple broadly neutralizing antibodies recognizing the fusion loop. Nevertheless, we found that several glycan cap-, GP base-, and HR2-directed antibodies cross-reacted and neutralized BDBV DRC/2026 GP pseudovirus with potency comparable or greater to that observed against earlier BDBV isolates and the Zaire ebolavirus Makona/2024 isolate. These findings define the antigenic properties of contemporary BDBV GP and delineate conserved epitopes as ideal targets for antibody therapeutics and for the development of pan-ebolavirus vaccines.

title: Ebola Virus Disease in Pregnancy: Maternal–Fetal Outcomes, Vertical Transmission, and Implications for Vaccination—A Narrative Review
abstract: Background/Objectives: Ebola virus disease (EVD) during pregnancy is associated with severe maternal illness and exceptionally poor fetal and neonatal outcomes. However, pregnancy-specific evidence remains limited by small cohorts, heterogeneous outbreak settings, and the historical exclusion of pregnant women from clinical research. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on maternal, fetal, and neonatal outcomes, placental involvement and vertical transmission, clinical management, and vaccination during pregnancy. Methods: PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar were searched from inception through May 2026 using predefined terms related to EVD, pregnancy, maternal and neonatal outcomes, placental infection, vertical transmission, and vaccination. WHO and CDC guidance documents and reference lists of relevant publications were also reviewed. Two reviewers independently screened records and assessed full texts. Data was extracted using a standardized template and independently verified by a second reviewer. A total of 55 publications met the inclusion criteria and were narratively synthesized. Results: Historical reports documented very high maternal mortality and pregnancy loss; however, more recent studies do not indicate that pregnancy independently increases maternal mortality among patients with EVD. A systematic review and meta-analysis estimated maternal mortality at 67.8% (95% CI 49.8–83.7), fetal loss at 76.9% (95% CI 45.0–98.3), and neonatal mortality at 98.5% (95% CI 84.9–100). Contemporary data from the 2018–2020 Democratic Republic of the Congo outbreak similarly found no increased maternal mortality associated with pregnancy, although fetal and perinatal outcomes remained poor. Evidence supports placental involvement in EVD, but placental viral RNA detection should be distinguished from confirmed fetal or neonatal infection. Pregnancy-specific vaccine evidence now includes a Phase 3 trial of Ad26.ZEBOV/MVA-BN-Filo in 2013 pregnant women, demonstrating favorable safety and immunogenicity profiles. Conclusions: EVD in pregnancy remains associated with substantial pregnancy loss and neonatal mortality despite improvements in maternal care. Important gaps persist regarding maternal–fetal transmission, long-term infant outcomes, and optimal management strategies, highlighting the need for further research.

title: Assessing the Risk for Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak and Health System Response Capacity in Conflict-Affected Sudan
abstract: Background: Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) is a severe viral hemorrhagic fever with high case fatality rates. Ongoing regional outbreaks in Uganda and the DRC, combined with protracted armed conflict in Sudan since April 2023, increase vulnerability to importation and spread, putting Sudan at risk. Conflict has caused widespread health infrastructure destruction, healthcare worker displacement, and disruption of surveillance and laboratory systems. This study assesses Sudan’s risk of an EVD outbreak and national response capacity in the context of conflict. Methods: We reviewed peer-reviewed and grey literature using PubMed, Medline, Google Scholar, WHO, CDC, UNICEF, and UN OCHA reports. No time restrictions were applied. We applied a SWOT analysis framework to classify factors influencing EVD prevention, detection, preparedness, and response in conflict-affected Sudan. The analysis focused on health system functionality, surveillance, laboratory capacity, workforce, and population vulnerabilities. Results: Our study found existing strengths, including availability of national EVD preparedness plans, prior experience responding to cholera, dengue, measles, and COVID-19, functional coordination through the Health Cluster, and ongoing disease surveillance systems including EWARS and Event-Based Surveillance. Weaknesses identified include severe disruption of health services (48% of facilities fully functional), health workforce shortages and burnout, disruption of laboratory capacity, and surveillance and access constraints in conflict-affected areas of Darfur and Kordofan. The ongoing health security frameworks, including the National Health Policy, National Health Sector Recovery Plan, and regional cross-border initiatives, expansion of digital surveillance, laboratory decentralization efforts, and recent international investments in health system recovery, provide significant opportunities for optimal preparedness and response. Threats identified include continued armed conflict and insecurity, large-scale internal displacement and cross-border mobility, humanitarian access constraints, and funding instability. Geographic risk synthesis indicates Darfur is at the highest risk for delayed detection and silent transmission, Kordofan serves as a transmission corridor, and Khartoum faces the highest risk of urban amplification. Conclusion: Sudan faces a moderate to high EVD outbreak risk due to potential virus importation, a conflict-weakened health system, and mass displacement. Key priorities: strengthen EWARS in conflict zones, decentralize laboratory capacity, restore health facilities with strong IPC, build workforce capacity, and adopt mobility-informed preparedness. Peace and international support remain essential for effective EVD response.

title: Epidemic response performance in contested territory: a comparative analysis of Ituri and North Kivu during the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak
abstract: Background. The 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is unfolding across provinces under materially different governance and security conditions. Ituri, the outbreak's epicentre, remains under national government administration despite insecurity; North Kivu's capital, Goma, and surrounding territory have been under March 23 Movement (M23)/Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC) control since early 2025. Existing published accounts treat insecurity as a generic, undifferentiated risk factor rather than isolating the specific contribution of contested territorial control. Methods. We compared Ituri and North Kivu on cumulative case fatality, health-zone coverage, and contact-tracing completeness using published, province-disaggregated surveillance figures from WHO, ECDC, and Africa CDC, contextualised against the documented conflict-related disruption of DRC's tenth Ebola outbreak (2018–2020), which affected the same two provinces. Two-proportion z-tests with 95% confidence intervals were used to test whether observed differences exceeded what chance alone would produce; the analysis is presented as hypothesis-generating throughout, consistent with the limits of an ecological design. Results. As of 7–8 August 2026, Ituri had reported 3,636 confirmed cases and 1,551 deaths (case fatality 42.7%) across 28 of 36 health zones; North Kivu had reported 470 cases and 315 deaths (case fatality 67.0%) across 12 of 34 health zones. North Kivu's contact-tracing follow-up (74.7%) fell below both the national figure (79.2%) and the 90–95% interruption threshold. The outbreak reached 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation, versus approximately 235 days for the 2018 outbreak in the same geography. The North Kivu-Ituri case-fatality gap (24.4 percentage points; 95% CI 19.8–28.9; z = 9.98, p < 0.001) was too large to reflect chance, but North Kivu's case fatality did not differ significantly from the 2018–2020 outbreak's final case fatality in the same geography (67.0% vs 66.0%; 95% CI -3.6 to 5.5 percentage points; p = 0.67), while Ituri's was significantly lower than that historical benchmark (42.7% vs 66.0%; p < 0.001), leaving epidemic-phase and case-ascertainment explanations fully consistent with the data. Conclusions. Contested territorial control is associated with, though not proven to independently cause, weaker outcome-linked response indicators; the gap is statistically robust but equally consistent with epidemic-phase and case-ascertainment differences, so this hypothesis-generating finding requires confirmation by time-matched, health-zone-level study before being treated as causal. Financing and access-negotiation strategies should be differentiated by governance geography, drawing explicitly on the documented lessons of the 2018–2020 outbreak in the same provinces.

Introduction and background The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has now experienced seventeen recognised Ebola outbreaks since the virus was first identified near the Ebola River in 1976, more than any other country (1). Ebola virus disease is a severe, often fatal illness caused by viruses of the family Filoviridae, of which Bundibugyo virus is one of six recognised species (2). The 2026 outbreak, caused by Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) rather than the more familiar Zaire ebolavirus, was declared on 15 May 2026 in Ituri Province, was declared a public health emergency of international concern under the International Health Regulations two days later (3, 4), and within three months had become the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in DRC, surpassing the 2018–2020 Kivu epidemic (5, 6). The clinical and public health dimensions of the response have been reviewed elsewhere (7). By early August 2026 it had also become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record by at least one benchmark: it reached 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation, versus approximately 235 days for the 2018 outbreak (8). This outbreak is being fought on two fronts simultaneously: an epidemiological one, and a security one. Ituri Province and North Kivu Province, its principal secondary front, are both affected by active armed conflict, but not in the same way or degree. Multiple armed groups, including the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), the CODECO militia coalition, and the Rwanda-backed M23, operate across both provinces and have long constrained humanitarian access (9). What distinguishes North Kivu is a governance configuration with no real precedent in prior filovirus responses: since capturing Goma in early 2025 and expanding into Bukavu and Uvira, the AFC/M23 coalition has established a parallel administration headquartered in the province's largest city, operating alongside, rather than in coordination with, national health authorities (10, 11). Ituri, while also affected by insecurity, displacement, and armed- group activity tied to artisanal mining, has not experienced the same degree of territorial exclusion of the national government (9). Existing published accounts of this outbreak's response performance analyse financing and personnel constraints in aggregate, and describe insecurity, displacement, and mining-related population movement as generic risk factors present 'in areas affected by' the outbreak, without isolating their differential effect by governance status (9, 12). This is a consequential gap. If contested territorial control carries a specific, quantifiable operational cost distinct from insecurity in general, then response strategies calibrated to national or even provincial averages will systematically misallocate resources, treating a structural access problem as if it were a resourcing problem that additional funding alone could resolve. Page 4/17 This analysis has two aims: to isolate, using only published province-disaggregated surveillance data, the specific difference in response-function performance between a province where the national government retains administrative control (Ituri) and one where it does not (North Kivu); and to place that comparison in historical context using DRC's own most directly comparable precedent, the 2018– 2020 Ebola outbreak, which occurred in the same two provinces under conflict conditions that, while not identical, were similarly characterised by contested access, community mistrust, and direct attacks on the response. That episode was extensively documented in the peer-reviewed literature in a way the current outbreak has not yet been, offering an empirical benchmark against which the plausibility of an access-driven explanation for the current pattern can be assessed. The analysis proceeds in four parts: a context and problem analysis; an evidence and critical analysis presenting the province-level data, the historical comparison, and a triangulated interpretation; implications for policy and practice; and a conclusion. 2. Context and problem analysis 2.1 The eastern DRC conflict landscape Eastern DRC's conflict is not a backdrop to this outbreak; it is one of the most protracted, complex security crises in the world, predating both the current epidemic and its 2018–2020 predecessor. Decades of conflict have displaced more than five million people across Ituri, North Kivu, and South Kivu combined (13); more recent UN refugee agency figures put total national displacement at 8.2 million as of September 2025, projected to reach 9 million by end-2026, including 5.8 million internally displaced, concentrated in these eastern provinces (14). The conflict is financed partly through control of artisanal mining sites producing gold, tin, tungsten, and tantalum, and competition for these resources recurringly drives confrontation between armed groups, the state, and, since 2025, the AFC/M23 administration (9, 13). This mineral-linked population mobility directly complicates contact tracing, since exposed individuals may cross administrative and control-line boundaries between exposure and case investigation. Violence against health care is itself a persistent, independently documented feature of this landscape: in 2023 alone, over 100 armed groups were active across North Kivu, Ituri, South Kivu, and Tanganyika, and 115 incidents of violence against or obstruction of health care were recorded in DRC, including kidnappings of health workers and looting of medical supplies (15). 2.2 Territorial change since 2025 and its operational implications The AFC/M23 coalition's capture of Goma in January 2025, and subsequent expansion into Bukavu and Uvira, fundamentally altered the operating environment for any health response in North Kivu and South Kivu (10). OCHA reporting describes this territorial expansion as causing renewed displacement, while at times forcing hundreds of thousands of previously displaced families to return to areas that remain fragile and only partially serviced (10). A December 2025 MONUSCO report, cited in UN reporting on the outbreak, documented persistent violence across Ituri and North Kivu in the months preceding the Page 5/17 outbreak's declaration, including attacks on villages, health facilities, and displaced communities that killed hundreds of civilians; the same reporting noted that fighting and movement restrictions were already limiting civilian movement and disrupting essential services before the first BVD case was confirmed (16). Displacement attributable to the current period is substantial in its own right: independent reporting estimated nearly one million people displaced within North Kivu specifically, with roughly 100,000 newly displaced in the first quarter of 2026 alone, immediately before the outbreak's onset (11). 2.3 A governance configuration without precedent in filovirus response No prior Ebola or Marburg response, including the 2018–2020 DRC outbreak, has operated at scale inside territory under sustained administrative control of a non-state armed coalition maintaining a parallel civil administration. Field reporting describes AFC/M23 forces providing security for the movement's own authorities at the National Biomedical Research Institute (INRB) laboratory in Goma responsible for analysing suspected Bundibugyo virus specimens - illustrating how deeply the response's core diagnostic infrastructure is embedded within contested governance, rather than operating alongside or independently of it (9). Congolese officials have themselves raised concern that an effective national response requires disengagement of Rwandan-backed forces from health infrastructure, reflecting a political dimension to outbreak control with no equivalent in 2018–2020, when the state, whatever its operational weaknesses, retained undisputed nominal authority throughout the affected territory (11). 2.4 Why the 2018–2020 outbreak is the appropriate comparator DRC's tenth Ebola outbreak, declared on 1 August 2018 in North Kivu and later spreading into Ituri, is the most relevant historical comparator available, for three reasons. First, it occurred in the identical two provinces now most affected by BVD. Second, it was, at the time, the most conflict-affected Ebola response ever mounted, generating an unusually rich peer-reviewed literature on the operational and epidemiological consequences of insecurity, mistrust, and direct attacks on response infrastructure - literature that does not yet exist for the current outbreak. Third, its final outcome is fully known (declared over in June 2020, with 3,481 total cases and 2,299 deaths, a case fatality of 66.0%) (17), allowing its trajectory to be compared against the current, still-evolving outbreak without the interpretive uncertainty of comparing a completed epidemic with an ongoing one on ecological grounds alone. A further, more practical reason reinforces the first three: because the 2018–2020 response generated province- and health-zone-level operational data that were subsequently analysed and published, it is possible to compare not only aggregate outcomes but the specific response-function indicators - contact-tracing completeness, time to isolation, community-reported trust - this analysis uses to characterise the current outbreak, giving the comparison a like-for-like quality a more distant historical outbreak could not offer. The remainder of this analysis uses that precedent as an explicit, descriptive benchmark against which Page 6/17 the plausibility of the access-driven explanation for the current Ituri-North Kivu gap can be assessed - illustratively, not as a natural experiment or control group from which a causal effect of governance status could be formally estimated. 3. Evidence and critical analysis 3.1 Data sources and analytic approach We extracted province-level case counts, deaths, and contact-tracing coverage from WHO, ECDC, and Africa CDC situational reporting published between late July and early August 2026 (5, 6, 18). All figures used are as published in these sources; no individual-level or unpublished data were accessed. We compared Ituri and North Kivu on three metrics: cumulative case fatality (deaths/confirmed cases), the proportion of each province's health zones reporting confirmed cases, and contact-tracing follow-up coverage, the last drawn specifically from Africa CDC's province-disaggregated reporting (18). National case totals were independently cross-checked against an unaffiliated European national public health institute's aggregation of the same outbreak, which reported figures consistent with the WHO/ECDC series (19). We supplemented this current-outbreak comparison with a structured historical comparison against the 2018–2020 outbreak, drawing on the US CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report (MMWR) account of that outbreak's final case count and trajectory (20), WHO's own closing outbreak summary (17), and the peer-reviewed literature documenting conflict-related disruption to that response (21, 22, 23). Consistent with recognised principles of ecological study design, we treat the current- outbreak comparison as hypothesis-generating rather than causally definitive (24): differences observed cannot be attributed to territorial control status alone, given that the two provinces also differ in population density, road and health infrastructure, outbreak duration to date, and baseline health-system capacity, all of which independently affect response performance. 3.2 Current outbreak: province-level results As of 7–8 August 2026, Ituri Province had reported 3,636 confirmed cases and 1,551 deaths (case fatality 42.7%) across 28 of its 36 health zones; North Kivu had reported 470 confirmed cases and 315 deaths (case fatality 67.0%) across 12 of its 34 health zones (5). National contact-tracing follow-up reached 79.2% of the 18,276 registered contacts as of early August, but this masked substantial provincial variation: follow-up in North Kivu stood at 74.7% and in Haut-Uélé at 66.7%, both below the national figure and well below the 90–95% coverage threshold WHO technical guidance identifies as necessary to interrupt transmission (18, 25).
